nameStory: The ash-throated flycatcher gets its name from the soft gray coloring on its throat and chest, which resembles the pale gray color of wood ash. This dusty, muted tone helps distinguish it from its flashier cousin, the great crested flycatcher, which sports a bright yellow belly.
description: The ash-throated flycatcher is a medium-sized songbird in the tyrant flycatcher family, known for catching insects on the wing. These birds have a brownish back, pale gray throat and chest, and subtle yellow on the belly and under the tail. They're about the size of a house sparrow but with a longer tail and a slightly crested head that gives them an alert, perky appearance.

idTips.label: Gray throat and chest
idTips.description: Look for the soft, ash-gray coloring on the throat and upper chest that gives this bird its name - it has a powdery, dusty appearance rather than bright white

idTips.label: Brownish back and wings
idTips.description: The back appears warm brown to grayish-brown, with darker brown wing feathers that show subtle rufous edges when seen up close

idTips.label: Pale yellow belly
idTips.description: The lower belly and undertail coverts show a soft, buttery yellow - much paler and more subtle than the bright yellow of great crested flycatchers

idTips.label: Slightly crested head
idTips.description: The head feathers can be raised into a small, peaked crest when the bird is alert or excited, giving it a distinctive silhouette

idTips.label: Upright perching posture
idTips.description: Sits very upright on exposed branches with tail hanging straight down, often flicking its tail and turning its head to scan for flying insects

idTips.label: Dark bill and legs
idTips.description: The bill appears black with a slightly hooked tip typical of flycatchers, while the legs are dark gray to black

habitat: In New England, ash-throated flycatchers are extremely rare visitors, typically found in open woodlands, forest edges, and areas with scattered trees and shrubs. When they do appear, it's usually during migration in places like coastal areas, parks, or woodland openings where they can hunt for flying insects from exposed perches.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants might appear in late May, usually single birds that are far from their normal western range.
seasonality.summer: Extremely uncommon in summer, with any sightings being notable vagrant records worth reporting to birding organizations.
seasonality.fall: Most New England records occur during fall migration from August through October, when birds occasionally wander far east of their typical range.
seasonality.winter: Not found in New England during winter months, as these birds migrate to warmer southern regions.

funFact: Ash-throated flycatchers are known to decorate their nests with unusual items like snake skins, cellophane, and even plastic wrap - the crinkly materials may help deter predators by making scary rustling sounds when the wind blows!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the great crested flycatcher, but ash-throated flycatchers have a gray (not white) throat and much paler yellow on the belly. Remember: 'Ash-throat = gray throat' versus 'Great crested = white throat with bright yellow belly.'
contextualKnowledge: The ash-throated flycatcher is primarily a western North American species, so any sighting in New England is considered a vagrant - a bird that has wandered far from its normal range. These rare appearances make them highly sought after by birders and are worth reporting to eBird or local birding groups.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the great crested flycatcher, the ash-throated flycatcher is smaller and much more subtly colored. While great crested flycatchers have bright white throats, lemon-yellow bellies, and bold rufous in the tail, ash-throated flycatchers are muted throughout with their signature gray throat and pale yellow belly. Great crested flycatchers are also much more common and expected in New England's deciduous forests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Great Crested Flycatcher is the only member of the Myiarchus genus regularly found in New England, making it unique among its close relatives here.
